course_title: Foundations in Politics, Policy and International Relations
course_description:
This course introduces students to the key ideas, issues, and modes of critical thought for study in political science and international studies. We provide the foundational content necessary for the study of governance and public policy, international relations, development, and peace and conflict studies through seminar discussions and individual and group projects. Topics to be examined include the problems of war, the economy, the rise of populism, inequality, and other pressing global and local problems using a variety of lenses drawn from international relations, governance and public policy, and peace and conflict studies.

There is no assumed background for completing this course.

course_aims: This course aims to introduce students to the ideas, issues and modes of critical thought relevant to Governance and Public Policy, International Relations, Peace and Conflict Studies, and Development. Upon completing POLS7002, students should demonstrate the type of understanding and knowledge necessary to complete more advanced courses in the field of politics.

learning_outcomes.description: Demonstrate a well-founded knowledge of the key ideas and issues in the field of politics.
Demonstrate acquired conceptual and analytical capacities, along with an ability to apply these skills to understand concrete social, political and historical processes in politics.
Develop intellectual tools and skills that will make you more competitive in your future professional activities in a variety of fields and positions.

assessment_details.title: Reflections
assessment_details.task_description: In weeks 1-12, students will spend 10 minutes writing a reflection on that week's content and seminar discussion. Each reflection is worth up to 2.5 marks, and should comprise a broader summary of the week's content (1 mark) and analysis/personal reflection (1.5 marks). Students' best 8 attempts will be recorded in Gradebook (for a maximum of 20 marks). More information about the reflections will be provided in the first class of the semester. This assessment task is to be completed in-person. The use of generative Artificial Intelligence (AI) or Machine Translation (MT) tools will not be permitted. Any attempted use of AI or MT may constitute student misconduct under the Student Code of Conduct. Read full task description Hide full task description

assessment_details.submission_guidelines:
Reflections will be handwritten, without the use of notes, and submitted to the course coordinator at the end of class.

Unfortunately, there are no opportunities for alternative assessment, except in the case of a Student Action Plan (SAP) or valid medical certificate. If absence is unavoidable, students must email the course coordinator before class. Students are reminded that only their best 8 attempts contribute to their mark for the semester.

assessment_details.title: Essay plan
assessment_details.task_description: In this task, students will produce an essay plan of no more than 1500 words . The course coordinator will provide feedback on the plan that students will then incorporate into their essay. The plan should include: Your essay title/topic An annotated bibliography, describing and critiquing at least 4 sources that help you demonstrate the gap or puzzle the essay will address The research question An argument plan, including your core argument and reasons in support of that argument An AI use case, detailing how and why AI will be used in the research and writing process, with reference to UQ policy and best practice More information about the essay plan assessment will be available on Blackboard, and we will discuss the essay plan in class in more detail. This task has been designed to be challenging, authentic and complex. Whilst students may use AI and/or MT technologies, successful completion of assessment in this course will require students to critically engage in specific contexts and tasks for which artificial intelligence will provide only limited support and guidance. A failure to reference generative AI or MT use may constitute student misconduct under the Student Code of Conduct. To pass this assessment, students will be required to demonstrate detailed comprehension of their written submission independent of AI and MT tools. Read full task description Hide full task description
assessment_details.assessment_security: Open assessment: In this assessment you can use resources such as your notes, course materials, and other tools, including AI, while completing the task. The focus is not on memorising information, but on understanding, applying judgement, and demonstrating your own thinking.
assessment_details.submission_guidelines:
Students should submit their essay plan via the Turnitin link on Blackboard.
Assignments for this course will be submitted electronically via Blackboard and using Turnitin .
In uploading an assignment via Turnitin you are certifying that it is your original work, that it has not been copied in whole or part from another person or source except where this is properly acknowledged, and that it has not in whole or part been previously submitted for assessment in any other course at this or any other university.
When you successfully submit your assessment to Turnitin after previewing the uploaded document (to make sure that you have chosen the correct file), you should see the “Submission Complete!” message. After this, a downloadable Digital Receipt will display on your Assignment Dashboard. It is your responsibility to download the Digital Receipt as proof of submission. Turnitin will not send this receipt to you automatically.
If you don’t see the downloadable receipt on your assignment dashboard, you should regard your submission as unsuccessful.
If the submission was not successful:
Note the error message (preferably take a screenshot). Go to your assignment page and see if it is possible to submit again. If you cannot submit again, then email your course coordinator immediately.
Deferral or extension
You may be able to apply for an extension .
The maximum extension allowed is 28 days. Extensions are given in multiples of 24 hours.
Late submission
A penalty of 10% of the maximum possible mark will be deducted per 24 hours from time submission is due for up to 7 days. After 7 days, you will receive a mark of 0.
Unless an extension is granted, penalties for late submission apply. Students are penalised 10% of the maximum possible mark allocated for the assessment item for every calendar day that an assessment item is late.
Marks will be deducted each day for up to 7 calendar days, at which point the submitted item will not receive any marks unless an extension has been approved. Each 24-hour block is triggered from the time the submission is due.

assessment_details.title: Essay (with hurdle)
assessment_details.task_description: Students will write a 3,000 word essay on one of the topics from the course. It is expected that students will make some small original research contribution. Emphasis should be on assessing relevant literature, identifying a gap in the literature, and how your research fills this gap. Further details and examples will be provided in class throughout the year. This task has been designed to be challenging, authentic and complex. Whilst students may use AI and/or MT technologies, successful completion of assessment in this course will require students to critically engage in specific contexts and tasks for which artificial intelligence will provide only limited support and guidance. Following essay submission, students will complete a short oral hurdle assessment in week 13, comprising a short presentation of the essay and responses to 1-2 follow up questions. More information about this assessment, including the assessment schedule, will be available on Blackboard in due course. Read full task description Hide full task description

learning_activities.topic: Week 1: What is politics? In this introductory seminar we will discuss some of the fundamental building blocks of what makes something political. Learning outcomes: L01, L02, L03
Week 2: Realism The next three seminars will examine some traditions/schools of thought in International Relations. This week we will introduce Realism. Learning outcomes: L01, L02, L03
Week 3: Liberalism This week we will examine Liberalism and how it emerged from a critique of how Realist scholars theorize anarchy. Learning outcomes: L01, L02, L03
Week 4: Constructivism This seminar will examine Constructivism and how ideas, norms, and social interactions can structure security and economic relations. Learning outcomes: L01, L02, L03
Week 5: Postcolonialism In this seminar we look at influential theories of postcolonial and Indigenous scholars. Learning outcomes: L01, L02, L03
Week 6: No class No class. Work on your essay plans, which are due on 4 September. Learning outcomes: L01, L02, L03
Week 7: Migration We analyze migration’s economic and political drivers, ethical dilemmas, and governance challenges in a globalized world. Learning outcomes: L01, L02, L03
Week 8: Domestic politics We begin by examining the seminal text Exit, Voice, and Loyalty and examine if non-violent civil resistance can be effective. Learning outcomes: L01, L02, L03
Week 9: Gender & inequality This week highlights how gender and economic inequality intersect with political systems and global governance. Learning outcomes: L01, L02, L03
Week 10: Contemporary conflicts We analyse recent conflicts, including the war in Ukraine, and their broader geopolitical and security implications. Learning outcomes: L01, L02, L03

Week 11: Essay workshop This week, we will participate in an essay workshop. In the first half, I will provide some essay writing tips and tricks. In the second half, students will present their essays to their peers in small groups, and exchange constructive feedback, critiques, and provocations. Learning outcomes: L01, L02, L03
Week 12: Environmental politics We will examine international climate politics and the distributive conflicts shaping climate policies. Learning outcomes: L01, L02, L03

Week 13: Oral assessments This week, students will undertake the oral assessment component of their essay. Students will not be required to attend the whole class. A timetable for attendance will be posted on Blackboard in due course. Learning outcomes: L01, L02, L03
